newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Greencore sees tough H2, rosier times ahead.
newsitem.headline: Greencore sees tough H2, rosier times ahead.

text.p: Irish sugar, milling and malting company Greencore Group Plc said on Wednesday it faced a difficult second-half in its current financial year but its longer term profit outlook was buoyant.

"Despite the fact that the second half will be a little weaker than people either anticipated or would wish, we will also demonstrate a very good operating performance in our businesses," chief executive David Dilger told a news conference after Greencore's first-half results.
Greencore reported interim profits of 21.71 million Irish pounds, down from 25.52 million in the same period the previous year. Its profits were hit by an exceptional charge of 5.8 million.
The company said full-year pre-exceptional profits would be "somewhat lower" than the previous year.

Dilger said second-half performance would be damaged by two main factors -- a boycott of its fertiliser products sparked by a dispute with growers, and an eight-week strike which hit sugar operations.

He said that although both disputes had now been solved, the boycott "has been painful for the business, particularly in the second half", while the strike would have a "significant cost in the early part of the second half".

Dilger said that while Greencore was on the lookout for acquisitions, it would only buy companies which fitted in with its skill base. He said he would announce "modest progress in the relatively near future" on the acquisitions front.

He said that Greencore would have to strengthen its foothold in the U.S. market in the longer term but had no plans to increase its 27-percent stake in U.S. sugar company Imperial Holly Corp in the near term.
Finance director Kevin O'Sullivan said the strength of the Irish pound had damaged turnover and profits in the first half. But he said there were signs that the currency situation was improving.

"There is some sign that the worst of the currency situation may have moderated," O'Sullivan said. "The pendulum may have reached one side and is going back. That would be positive for us going forward."
